doc.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Avoiding studio work; the Beehive Lounge house band
summary: He explains why he skipped studio work, then recalls the Beehive Lounge house band accompanying visiting stars such as Charlie Parker.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: blues, maybe that’s something in the back of my mind as to why I don’t have that much music. I have some tunes you know. Occasionally I let them work on a bebop tune and let an ensemble do it, but other than that I just sort of got away from it. I was never that interested in getting back to it. I was never interested; and doing studio work, which is probably the most lucrative part of the business you know. Like look at the studio musicians now, even those into retirement, man they have pensions in five and six figures. Mine is barely in three figures you know. But studio work is like a nine to five job to me. It’s done mostly in the daytime where you have to be in the studio early, and you’re always playing somebody else’s music. And that doesn’t — I won’t say it rubs the wrong way, but I think I would get very bored playing. And I just never pursued playing studio music. Even though I was asked, “Why don’t you think about it?” But I think another thing too, because I was playing with so many of my heroes when I was young, so many of my idols, like Lester Young, and Gene Ammons of course and Leo Parker, the late Leo Parker, the baritone player. And then when I got out of the Army I had this gig at the Beehive Lounge in Chicago, where I was with the house band with Israel Crosby on bass, another local drummer named Buddy Smith playing drums, and they brought in singles, like Charlie Parker worked there for a month, shoot one time I worked with Charlie Parker. He was one of the people that influenced me to come to New York. On the gig he says, “You should come to New York.” And when I finally showed up in New York I ran into him one day downtown, and he says, “So you finally made it” he was telling me and I said, “Yep, I’m here to stay, too.” And people like that, Coleman Hawkins played the Beehive, Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis, Sonny Stitt, just about everybody you can name. And they all came without groups. And this club would book them for at least a month.
